title: tat tvam asi
tomorrow: what if the line really says 'you are NOT that'?

segments.voice: Yesterday, tat tvam asi the Advaita way: this is that Devadatta, the labels set aside on both sides. Today, a second school, and a strange sentence it leans on.

A phone runs on code nobody using it ever sees. It's in every tap, and the phone has no idea. The Brihadaranyaka Upanishad has a stranger sentence than that. The father from the Chandogya, Uddalaka Aruni, presses the sage Yajnavalkya about the inner controller. The answer: the one who dwells in the earth, whom the earth does not know, whose body the earth is. How can something live in the earth, and the earth not know it?
screen: `CODE YOU NEVER SEE.` → `THE INNER CONTROLLER.` → `IN THE EARTH, UNKNOWN TO IT?`

segments.voice: In paraphrase, Yajnavalkya says: the one who dwells in the earth, yet is other than the earth, whom the earth does not know, whose body the earth is, who rules the earth from within, that is your self, the inner controller, the immortal. Then he goes through water, fire, sky, wind, sun, breath, eye and mind, the same pattern each time. Here's the answer to the puzzle. A body doesn't have to know who lives in it to be lived in. Ramanuja, the teacher of the Vishishtadvaita school, reads tat tvam asi through this passage. Everything, your own self included, is the body of Brahman, and Brahman lives in it as its inner self. Now think about names. Say Devadatta, and you don't mean a body alone; you mean the person who has that body. So in Ramanuja's reading, you finally names Brahman too: Brahman as the one whose body you are. That names Brahman as the cause of the world. One reality, named two ways, and nothing set aside. Your self stays real, and stays yours, held as close as a body and the one who lives in it. For Ramanuja, the saying doesn't erase the one who hears it. It tells them who lives within them.
screen: `IN THE EARTH, UNKNOWN TO THE EARTH.` · `THE INNER CONTROLLER.` · `YOU ARE BRAHMAN'S BODY.` · then, large: `NOTHING SET ASIDE.`

segments.voice: Sit tall and feel the body from the inside: the weight in the seat, the breath moving, the warmth in the hands. Let the ground under you and the air around you belong to the same picture. If you pray, you can rest with the text's own words: the inner controller, the immortal.
Tat tvam asi, read Ramanuja's way: both words name Brahman, and you are the body it dwells in.
Here's the line: tat tvam asi, one reality, named two ways, nothing set aside. Talk soon.

howItsDone: In the Sri Vaishnava tradition that follows Ramanuja, the inner-controller passage of the Brihadaranyaka is studied as a key to reading the Upanishads, and the self is understood as the body of Brahman.

sources.ref: Brihadaranyaka Upanishad 3.7.1–3 and following (Uddalaka Aruni asks Yajnavalkya about the inner controller; the one who dwells in the earth, other than the earth, whom the earth does not know, whose body the earth is, who rules it from within: that is your self, the inner controller, the immortal)
Ramanuja, Vedartha Sangraha and Sri Bhashya on tat tvam asi (both words denote Brahman; 'tvam' denotes Brahman with the individual self as its body) — general

notes: The list in 3.7 (water, fire, sky, wind, sun, breath, eye, mind) is a selection; the lesson gives no count. Confirm the verse range (3.7.3 ff.) and that the Uddalaka of 3.7 is identified with Uddalaka Aruni of Chandogya 6 (the lesson says 'the father from the Chandogya').

Ramanuja's reading is summarized, not quoted: 'that' as Brahman the cause of the world; 'you' as Brahman with the individual self as its body; words for a body reaching to the self that has it. Confirm the summary and the Devadatta illustration as fair to his argument. 'Held as close as a body and the one who lives in it' is the lesson's plain rendering of the sharira–shariri relation.
The hook's phone-code picture is the lesson's own analogy for 'whom the earth does not know'; it is not meant to equate the inner controller with a mechanism.
